Here are some of the important technology stories from this week:
CoreWeave sell-off puts AI infrastructure financing under scrutiny
CoreWeave
shares plunged 12.80% on Friday as investors questioned the cost of expanding AI data centers. The
spread to Nebius
and IREN
amid concerns about borrowing costs and capital requirements.
CoreWeave's debt and lease obligations totaled approximately $52B at the end of June, highlighting the financial burden of its AI infrastructure expansion.
TSMC outlook signals resilient AI chip demand
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing
forecasted fourth-quarter revenue of $52.3B to $54.3B, above analysts' consensus of $50.48B, providing fresh evidence of resilient semiconductor demand.

high-performance computing revenue rose 22% quarter over quarter. Management said AI accelerator revenue growth could exceed its previous mid-to-high-50% CAGR forecast for 2024–2029, signaling continued demand despite the broader technology sell-off.
Anthropic IPO valuation expectations cool as growth slows
Anthropic's
anticipated initial public offering faces greater valuation scrutiny as investors assess its growth trajectory and AI development costs.
Reuters reported that some investors were discussing a potential valuation of around $1.5T, below earlier expectations of approximately $2T.

The AI company reportedly generated $16.8B in third-quarter revenue, up 45% sequentially, and was profitable on an adjusted basis. However, the slower growth rate disappointed some investors after revenue more than doubled from the first quarter to $11.6B in the second quarter.
The valuation discussions remain preliminary and do not represent confirmed IPO pricing.
AI spending pressures hyperscaler cash flow
Bank of America Global Research expects Microsoft
to be the only major hyperscaler among its comparison group not to enter negative free cash flow territory over the next 12 months.
Amazon
, Alphabet
, Oracle
, and Meta Platforms

are projected to face negative free cash flow as AI infrastructure investment continues. The firm expects cash generation to recover by the second half of 2027, assuming AI revenue accelerates and capital expenditure growth slows.
Bank of America sees memory-stock sell-off diverging from fundamentals
Bank of America analysts said the recent pullback in SK Hynix
and Samsung Electronics

may reflect fears of an AI spending slowdown rather than weakening memory fundamentals. Investors have worried about borrowing costs for AI cloud providers, potential Chinese supply growth, and the sustainability of demand.

BofA, however, expects memory prices, sales, and margins to remain strong through 2028. The divergence highlights uncertainty around the memory cycle: shares have come under pressure even as some forecasts point to continued demand and earnings strength.
Meta expands open AI model push with Muse Spark Open
Meta Platforms

released Muse Spark Open, an AI model designed for coding and complex tasks. It has 816B parameters, with 42B active during use, and its weights are available to developers. The model can run locally on suitably configured Apple
Mac Studio computers, expanding Meta's open-model offering.
